subject: Accounting
title: Lehman Brothers: Hidden Leverage
description: One-minute skill: Lehman Brothers: Hidden Leverage.

hook.text: In 2008, Lehman Brothers collapsed with $600 billion in assets. Nobody saw it coming.

buildup.text: Lehman's balance sheet showed acceptable leverage ratios just weeks before bankruptcy.

discovery.text: A trick called 'Repo 105' temporarily moved $50 billion of debt off the books each quarter.

twist.text: Auditors knew. They signed off anyway. The clean audit opinion masked the catastrophe.

climax.text: Lehman's collapse triggered the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

punchline.text: Clean books don't always mean clean business.

quiz.question: What did Lehman's 'Repo 105' trick do?
options: Temporarily removed debt from the balance sheet

details.summary: Lehman Brothers used an accounting maneuver called Repo 105 to temporarily remove $50 billion in assets from its balance sheet before each reporting date, masking its true leverage. This topic covers the technique and how it contributed to the 2008 financial crisis.
details.whyItMatters: Lehman Brothers demonstrates how financial institutions can use legal accounting techniques to deceive investors and regulators about their true risk level, with catastrophic systemic consequences.
takeaways: Repo 105 treated short-term borrowing as a sale, temporarily removing assets from the balance sheet
This made Lehman's leverage appear lower at each quarter-end than it actually was during the quarter
Lehman's collapse in September 2008 triggered the most severe global financial crisis since the Great Depression

faq.question: What was Lehman Brothers' Repo 105?
faq.answer: Repo 105 was a repurchase agreement where Lehman pledged assets worth at least 105% of the cash received, allowing it to classify the transaction as a 'sale' rather than a loan. This temporarily removed up to $50 billion from the balance sheet at each quarter-end.

faq.question: How did hidden leverage contribute to Lehman's collapse?
faq.answer: By masking its true leverage, Lehman prevented market participants from seeing how exposed it was to declining mortgage assets. When the mortgage market collapsed, Lehman's actual leverage was far higher than reported, making the losses unsurvivable.
